contributions: Naming and formalizing multiplicity-induced structure-level credit concentration, with the aggregate coefficient assigned to a recurring form written explicitly as its count times the shared base advantage

Separating the two design decisions that prior work conflates — how verified-correct completions are partitioned, and how positive credit is redistributed once they are — so each can be tested independently
A partition-conditioned redistribution rule with a rarity exponent, normalized so the mean positive multiplier is unchanged and incorrect-completion advantages are left entirely alone
A deterministic partition from a fixed catalogue of 27 symbolic and natural-language cues extracted from the traces themselves, requiring no auxiliary-model inference at training time
A control applying the same redistribution rule to a judge-derived partition, which is what shows the mechanism is not tied to the cue instantiation
limitations: The paper has no limitations section. What a reader should weigh: the multi-seed table shows gains of +1.90, +2.86 and +0.63 at the largest budget and mean gains under one point at smaller ones, so the headline is a high-budget effect with seed-level variance comparable to its size at ordinary budgets. The cue catalogue is fixed for competition mathematics and the authors say extending it to richer structural representations is future work, so the partition mechanism as instantiated is domain-specific even though the redistribution rule is not. Training is LoRA on 1,000 problems for one epoch on a single GPU, which bounds what the comparison establishes about full finetuning at scale. The rarity exponent, similarity threshold and clipping range are one fixed configuration across backbones — commendable — but were chosen somewhere, and the ablation that selects the exponent runs on the same benchmark the headline reports. And the mechanism diagnostic shows the realized exponent (0.72) is far from the theoretical one (0.2), so clipping and singleton handling, not the rarity rule alone, determine the actual weight distribution.
method: For each prompt a group of completions is sampled and verified by a rule-based checker. Verified-correct completions are partitioned by cue signature: each trace is segmented into steps, each step is labelled with the highest-priority matching cue from a fixed catalogue defined before training and never tuned on an evaluation benchmark, consecutive duplicates and generic labels are removed, and cues shared by more than a threshold fraction of the group are suppressed so the signature reflects what distinguishes completions rather than what they share. Signatures become count vectors, cosine similarity above a threshold defines a graph, and its connected components are the clusters. Positive advantages are then reweighted by cluster size raised to the negative rarity exponent and renormalized so the average multiplier stays at one, with anomalous singleton clusters reset, multipliers clipped to a fixed range and a minimum positive multiplier applied. Incorrect completions keep their original negative advantages and the standard objective, clipping, KL term and optimizer are unchanged. Training uses LoRA on a math-specialized 7B backbone over 1,000 competition problems with 64 completions per prompt, and a general 8B instruction model as a second family; evaluation is repeated-sampling pass@k summarized as normalized area under the pass@k curve, at up to 256 completions per problem.
one_liner: Shows that GRPO's per-completion uniformity is frequency-skewed once credit is aggregated by solution structure — a recurring correct form accumulates positive coefficient mass proportional to how often it is sampled — and rebalances it by a rarity exponent over a partition built from deterministic cue signatures rather than a judge model.
problem: Under binary rewards every verified-correct completion in a group receives the same positive base advantage, which looks uniform. It is not uniform at the level that matters: if the same underlying solution form appears many times in a rollout group, that form accumulates total positive coefficient mass in proportion to its multiplicity, while a rare correct form receives only the credit of its few instances. That allocation is consistent with expected-reward optimization and poorly aligned with high-budget repeated sampling, where keeping alternative correct modes alive is what improves the odds on hard problems. Prior work addressing this either optimizes a pass@k objective directly or groups completions with an auxiliary judge model, the latter making the partition entirely dependent on the judge's outputs and requiring substantial inference throughout training.

relevance.reasoning-training: It identifies a bias in GRPO that is invisible at the level the objective is written: per-completion uniformity becomes frequency-skew once credit is summed over recurring solution structures, so the update systematically favours the modes a policy already prefers. That is a mechanism for the entropy and diversity collapse this archive tracks, stated in terms of credit rather than of entropy, and it is measurable — the fitted slope of cluster credit mass against cluster size is 1.00 under GRPO and can be moved. The random-partition ablation is the result most worth carrying, and it is the third time this archive has seen its shape: a randomized control captures half the benefit attributed to a targeted criterion, alongside a random-position clip matching a covariance-targeted one and a reward-free random walk in latent space nearly matching a reward-guided method. Any RLVR credit-assignment claim in this archive should now be expected to run a randomized-partition or random-direction control before the criterion is credited. The paper also keeps a discipline worth noting: the redistribution touches only positive advantages and leaves the negative branch untouched, which is the same constraint the archive's other credit-assignment work arrived at from a different direction.

results: The clearest gains are on the hardest benchmark, where single-sample accuracy is low and repeated correct forms are exposed at large budgets: area under pass@k improves over GRPO at every reported budget on the 7B backbone (30.62 to 32.06 at 64, 34.99 to 37.00 at 128, 39.89 to 42.75 at 256), and the same pattern holds on the 8B general model (18.85 to 19.77 and 23.92 to 25.71). On near-saturated benchmarks differences are small, consistent with a method targeting positive-credit allocation rather than single-sample accuracy — and the paper reports where it loses, with the judge-based baseline best on one benchmark at all three budgets and vanilla GRPO or that baseline ahead on two of the 8B results. Coverage moves in the right direction without being uniformly better: at 256 samples the method solves 8 problems GRPO never solves while GRPO uniquely solves 4, with a mean paired difference of +2.52 correct completions per problem (two-sided sign test p = 0.049). The mechanism check confirms the intended change rather than assuming it — under GRPO cluster-level positive credit grows linearly with cluster size (fitted slope 1.00), and the method reduces that to 0.72, with singleton clusters receiving 1.43 times their GRPO mass and the largest clusters 0.46 times. Overhead is about 6% of per-step wall clock against roughly 62% for the judge-based alternative. The ablations are the most informative part and one of them cuts against the paper's own framing: uniformly boosting every correct advantage recovers only 0.49 of the 3.55-point gain, but partitioning at *random* and applying the same redistribution recovers 1.45 — so half the benefit survives destroying the semantic content of the partition, and the cue-derived grouping adds a further 2.10 on top. A variant that removes the additive floor and renormalizes to unit mean preserves 68% of the improvement, ruling out a simple increase in average positive-credit scale as the explanation. Across three seeds the gain at the largest budget averages +1.80 and is smaller and less consistent at 64 and 128, which the authors state directly: the benefit is most reliable at high sampling budgets.
